newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: EU crude oil stocks draw in May comes as surprise.
newsitem.headline: EU crude oil stocks draw in May comes as surprise.

text.p: The fall of European Union crude oil stocks in May came as a surprise, while product levels were in line with expectations, re-enforcing the oversupply of distillates, analysts said on Tuesday.
The figures came in Euroilstock's monthly report of inventories in the 15 countries of the European Union plus Norway.
Analysts questioned before Tuesday's publication of the report all said they expected crude stocks to have risen last month, albeit not by as much as the 13 million barrel gain in April.
However, crude oil stocks fell in May, by 3.65 million barrels, or 0.8 percent, to 429.24 million barrels, leaving them 250,000 barrels lower than year-ago levels.
Most of the month-on-month fall was in the three country grouping Finland/Norway/Sweden where crude stocks declined by 3.21 million barrels.
The crude fall came despite slightly lower crude intake. Refineries used 190,000 barrels per day less than in April.
Analysts speculated that North Sea maintenance may have had a greater effect than originally thought and that much crude exported from regions such as West Africa had steered clear of Europe.

"Europeans are obviously not buying the crude. It confirms the view that European companies are looking to cut costs. It's a low growth market for oil and they have all the supplies they need," said Peter Bogin of Cambridge Energy Research Associates.
While the crude stock draw needed some explaining, product stock movements were in accordance with seasonal norms.
Middle distillate stocks rose by 4.95 million barrels, or 1.6 percent, to 316.88 million barrels.
Analysts said the combination of lower demand from the Asia Pacific region after large-scale buying in April and little sign of improved German buying explained the stocks rise.
"There was no evidence of great demand anywhere in May," said Leslie Owens of Petroleum Economics.
The year-on-year surplus also increased -- from 11.89 million barrels in April to 19.54 million barrels in May.
"Middle distillates were already very high. The overhang has clearly just grown," said Geoff Pyne, oil analyst at bank UBS.
Gasoline inventories offered few surprises, dropping by 5.95 million barrels, or 3.6 percent, in May to 160.99 million barrels. They were 4.27 million barrels, or 2.6 percent, lower than a year ago.
Crude and oil product stocks combined fell by 7.39 million barrels, or 0.7 percent, to 1,081.27 million barrels at the end of May.
